content: Feeding preterm or low birth weight newborns was encouraged either through gavage or cup feeding, or by breastfeeding. Early initiation and gradual escalation of feeding were promoted to minimize the need for intravenous fluids. Infection prevention and management were emphasized, including strict handwashing protocols upon entering neonatal intensive care units, hand sanitization between patient contacts, and the use of disposable materials whenever possible. Staff were trained to identify signs of infection and potential sepsis, and antibiotic stewardship was encouraged in neonatal units. Kangaroo mother care was recommended for all preterm and low birth weight infants, with some hospitals providing dedicated rooms adjacent to neonatal care units for this purpose. In most hospitals, surfactant therapy and mechanical ventilation were not available for managing preterm infants, and these interventions were not part of the respiratory support provided in the trial. These medications needed to be readily accessible in antenatal, labor, and emergency obstetric wards. Simplified administration protocols and standardized communication regarding dosing and handover were also recommended. Local guidelines and clinical protocols were adapted through a multi-stakeholder, consensus-driven process to align with WHO, national, sub-national, and facility-level standards. National guidelines included clear criteria for the appropriate use and acceptable regimens of antenatal corticosteroids, addressing specific conditions such as diabetes or fetal growth restriction. Training for healthcare professionals on safe and appropriate use of antenatal corticosteroids, gestational age dating via ultrasound, and preterm newborn care (including resuscitation, oxygen therapy, CPAP, thermal care, breastfeeding, glucose monitoring, infection prevention, and kangaroo mother care) was emphasized. Educational materials, decision aids, and reminder systems were made accessible to healthcare professionals. Key performance indicators, audits, and feedback mechanisms were implemented to monitor the use of antenatal corticosteroids. Change champions or opinion leaders were appointed to promote their appropriate use. Effective implementation of these recommendations required reorganization of care and redistribution of healthcare resources, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Barriers such as limited gestational age estimation, lack of referral mechanisms, and inadequate care pathways for preterm labor and newborns were identified. Local protocols were developed to integrate the management of women at high risk of preterm birth and preterm newborns, with attention to contextual factors influencing survival. Accurate pregnancy dating during early antenatal visits was prioritized, and healthcare staff were trained to estimate gestational age and recognize clinical features of spontaneous preterm labor. Other aspects of maternal and newborn care quality, such as radiant warmers and kangaroo mother care, were also considered. Clear referral pathways for women at high risk of preterm birth were established within healthcare facilities. Monitoring and evaluation of guideline implementation were conducted at health service, regional, and country levels using defined criteria and indicators aligned with local targets. Data collection and evaluation were performed in collaboration with WHO teams to assess the impact on national policies. Research priorities included understanding barriers and facilitators to antenatal corticosteroid use in low-resource settings, evaluating benefits and risks for late preterm births, determining optimal regimens and dosing intervals, and addressing long-term outcomes for infants exposed to antenatal corticosteroids. Strategies to support shared decision-making and equitable distribution of benefits were also explored. The WHO regularly reviews maternal and perinatal health recommendations to prioritize updates based on new evidence. Concerns about the validity of recommendations are promptly addressed, and suggestions for additional research questions are welcomed.
